source_refs.note: Topic 2.7.4, printed page 36: Hund's rule with the printed right and wrong arrangements.

blocks.text: This rule gives an idea for filling electrons into the orbitals having equal energies. For example, three p-orbitals, i.e., px, py and pz have equal energy. To understand it, let us take an example in which three electrons are to be filled into three p-orbitals. There are two different ways to do this as shown below:

blocks.alt: Two ways of placing three electrons in the px, py and pz boxes. I (wrong): two electrons with opposite spins in px, one in py, pz empty. II (right): one electron in each of px, py and pz, all with the same spin.
blocks.caption: Hund's rule: I (wrong) and II (right) filling of px, py and pz (original drawing after the textbook's uncaptioned diagram in topic 2.7.4).

blocks.text: Which of the two is correct? The answer is given by Hund’s rule, which states that,

blocks.title: Hund’s rule
blocks.text: When degenerate orbitals are available and more than two electrons are to be placed in them, they should be placed in separate orbitals with the same spin rather than in the same orbital with opposite spins.
According to the Hund’s rule, the correct way of filling three electrons in three p orbitals is that in which each orbital is singly occupied.
